slides.name: 35 · Seven things interaction lets a reader do

params.text: Seven things interaction lets a reader do

params.data:
Technique	The reader…	For example	In Altair
Select	marks something as interesting	highlight a country	selection_point
Explore	shows something else	pan and zoom	bind='scales'
Reconfigure	shows a different arrangement	re-sort the bars	a radio that changes the sort
Encode	shows a different representation	switch the measure	binding_select on a field
Abstract / elaborate	shows more or less detail	overview + detail; a tooltip	tooltip=, interval on x
Filter	shows something conditionally	only one region	transform_filter
Connect	shows related items	brushing and linking	the same selection in two charts

slides.notes: 3 min. The 2025 deck's list of core techniques. Its source is Yi, Kang, Stasko & Jacko (2007), "Toward a deeper understanding of the role of interaction in information visualization" (the 2025 slide credited VAD 6.6–6.8; Munzner's own treatment is Chapter 11). Every row is in the guide: §5–13.

slides.name: 45 · Live figure · Spot the bug
slides.notes:
3 min. ASK first: "What went wrong?" Let them hover: each slice is a country.
WHY: in Vega-Lite every unaggregated field in the encoding (tooltip included) becomes a group-by key. Adding country:N to the tooltip of an aggregated bar splits it by country.
FIX: aggregate in the tooltip too (sum(population)), or aggregate first with transform_aggregate and tooltip the result. Guide §4.

LAB — A live figure, drawn here as its last step. The show plays the real one: the room can hover it and Next steps it.

figureData.guide: Your guide §4 · Aggregated marks need aggregated tooltips

figureSteps.caption: Population by region. Why is every bar sliced into pieces? Hover one.
country:N is not aggregated, so Vega groups by it too: one stacked bar per country.
The fix: an aggregate tooltip at the same grain as the bar. One bar, one card.

figure.title: Spot the bug
figure.figureAlt: A bar chart of population by region whose bars are sliced into countries, beside the Altair that made it.

slides.name: 46 · Where a tooltip fails

params.text: No hover on a phone: the card never opens
Label the key values; make the mark a tap target
A mouse-only card shuts out keyboard users
Native controls; values in a table or the caption
A picture keeps no hover at all
A deliberate static version, with labels (guide §17)
The point is only in the card
Put the message in the title; the card holds detail

slides.notes: 2 min. WCAG 2.1, 1.4.13 Content on Hover or Focus: content that appears on hover must be dismissable, hoverable and persistent, and reachable without a mouse.

slides.name: 49 · Live figure · Be the brush
slides.notes:
6 min. THE CENTREPIECE OF STOP 3. Drag and click live; invite a volunteer to the laptop for the brush.
Each step: the same strip. HOVER: input pointerover, parameter the country, predicate alt.when(hover), response colour. CLICK: input click, parameter a SET of countries (toggle). LEGEND: input a legend click, parameter a region. BRUSH: input a drag, parameter a RANGE of x and y; the bars use the same brush in transform_filter: that is linking.
EMPTY: Vega's default treats an empty selection as "all selected"; for highlight-on-hover you want empty=False, or everything is lit at the start.

slides.name: 50 · One grammar, every selection

params.data:
Interaction	Input	Parameter (what is stored)	Predicate	Visual response
Hover	pointer over a mark	one value: the country	alt.when(hover)	colour, size, stroke
Click	click (toggle=True)	a set of countries	alt.when(picked)	opacity
Legend	click on the legend	one region	alt.when(region)	opacity
Brush	drag	a range of x and y	alt.when(brush) / transform_filter(brush)	lit marks; filtered bars
Slider	drag a slider	a number: the year	alt.datum.year == year	the frame shown

slides.notes: 2 min. Names what they just did in Be the brush, as the strip. Only the input column changes much. The slider row is the one they already know: the Week 1 query, next but one.

slides.name: 51 · Build it: one brush, two views

params.text: Build it: one brush, two views

brush = alt.selection_interval()          # input: a drag; stored: a range of x and y

scatter = alt.Chart(world).mark_circle().encode(
    x=alt.X('income:Q', scale=alt.Scale(type='log')),
    y='health:Q',
    color=alt.when(brush)                 # test: is the mark inside the range?
        .then('region:N')                 # response: lit
        .otherwise(alt.value('lightgrey')),
).add_params(brush)

bars = alt.Chart(world).mark_bar().encode(
    x='count():Q',
    y='region:N',
).transform_filter(brush)                 # the second view answers the first

scatter | bars

slides.notes:
2 min. Guide §8–9. The whole of Be the brush's last steps in one cell. The brush is declared once, added to the scatter with add_params, and used twice: alt.when(brush) colours the scatter, transform_filter(brush) filters the bars. That second use is linking.
ASK: "Which line makes the views talk to each other?" transform_filter(brush). Before the first drag every mark is lit (empty=True, the default): add empty=False to start with nothing lit.

slides.name: 52 · You built a dynamic query in Week 1

params.text: You built a dynamic query in Week 1

year = alt.selection_point(
    name='year', fields=['year'], value=1955,
    bind=alt.binding_range(min=1955, max=2005, step=5))

alt.Chart(data.gapminder()).mark_circle().encode(
    x='fertility:Q',
    y='life_expect:Q',
    size='pop:Q',
    color='cluster:N',
    tooltip=['country:N', 'year:O'],
).add_params(year).transform_filter(year)

slides.notes: 2 min. The table's last row: they have built one already. From the Week 1 guide, §4 (Rosling with a year slider). INPUT the slider, PARAMETER the year, PREDICATE transform_filter keeps rows of that year, RESPONSE the frame. A widget is a selection whose input is an HTML control: binding_range, binding_select, binding_radio, binding_checkbox (guide §12).

slides.name: 56 · Section · When should a chart move?
slides.notes: 20 s. Animation: motion, transitions, change over time.

slides.name: 57 · Why animate a chart?

params.text: A state becoming another: before to after, one year to the next.
Motion is seen before almost anything else on the screen.
A tween lets the eye follow one item between two views.
A presenter can pace it: Rosling talks while the world moves.

slides.notes: 1 min. From the 2025 Week 5 deck: encode data, direct attention, understand dynamics and transitions, engagement.

slides.name: 58 · Motion is seen first

params.text: Motion reads as continuous at about 10 frames a second

Pre-attentive: stronger than colour or shape
Strongest in the corner of your eye
Things that move together are seen as a group

slides.notes: 1 min. From the 2025 deck's motion-perception slide (Zeki 1993). Common fate (Gestalt): what moves together is grouped. That is why a moving chart is powerful, and why a moving decoration is a distraction.

slides.notes: 1 min. A bar chart race: popular, and a good test. ASK: "What can you read here that you couldn't from a line chart? What can't you?" You see rank changes; you lose the values and the comparison across years. Fine to present, poor to analyse.

slides.name: 65 · Full picture
slides.notes: 1 min. The 2025 deck's pair (observablehq.com/blog/effective-animation): this and the election tween. ASK: "Which was easier to follow, and why?" The election tween changes one thing at a time; the storm moves a lot at once. (The map itself is next lecture.)

slides.name: 66 · Live figure · Frames or tweens?
slides.notes:
2 min. Both charts run on one clock, so nobody has to remember the first while watching the second. Iran crosses the whole chart, 7 babies and 41 years to under 2 and 74.
ASK while it plays: "Which one can you follow?" The right, because the eye tracks smooth motion; the left makes it find the bubble again after every jump.
NEXT: the trails stand still. ASK: "Which one is the data?" The dots: Gapminder measured every fifth year. The line is a tween: it invents every position in between.
Altair alone gives FRAMES: a slider changes the year and the chart redraws (guide §18). Smooth TWEENS need interpolated positions and a timer: the guide's player (§19). Be honest about which you are showing.

slides.name: 67 · Live figure · The UK became Bangladesh
slides.notes:
3 min. OBJECT CONSTANCY (Bostock, 2012). Without a key, Vega pairs old marks with new rows by their index. Here each year's rows arrive sorted by population, largest first. The UK is 8th in 1955; as Bangladesh, Pakistan and Nigeria grow past it, the 8th mark is a different country: Bangladesh in 1965, Pakistan in 1980, Japan in 2000, Nigeria in 2005. The red trail leaps across the chart.
With key='country:N' each mark is one country all the way through. In the guide: encode(..., key='borough:N') (§18).

slides.name: 68 · Build it: a year you can play

params.text: Build it: a year you can play

frame = alt.param(name='frame_year', value=1955)

alt.Chart(data.gapminder()).mark_circle().encode(
    x=alt.X('fertility:Q', scale=alt.Scale(domain=[0, 9])),
    y=alt.Y('life_expect:Q', scale=alt.Scale(domain=[25, 85])),
    size='pop:Q',
    color='cluster:N',
    key='country:N',              # identity: one mark, one country
).add_params(frame).transform_filter(
    alt.datum.year == frame       # the frame shown
)
# playback: a timer calls view.signal('frame_year', y)  (guide §19)

slides.notes: 2 min. Guide §18–19. Fixed domains so the axes do not jump between frames; key= for identity; a parameter for the year; transform_filter for the frame. Altair writes the chart; the guide's small player script drives the parameter on a timer (export_player).

slides.name: 71 · Live figure · Which country changed most?
slides.notes:
2 min. ASK after the animation: "Which country changed most?" Hard: animation asks you to remember the earlier frames. Munzner 6.5: Eyes Beat Memory.
Robertson et al. (2008): animation was the most enjoyed but the slowest and least accurate for analysis; small multiples and trails did better. Use animation to PRESENT change, small multiples to ANALYSE it.

slides.name: 72 · Animation: what it gives, what it costs

params.text: Animation: what it gives, what it costs
Cognitive overload when too much moves
Slower to read values; relies on memory
A reader alone cannot pause what is not pausable

slides.name: 73 · Design choices for animation

params.text: Know whether it is for communication, exploration or explanation
Transitions slow enough to follow, one change at a time
Too fast, too slow, or everything at once
Object constancy: key= so each mark stays itself
With users; compare against small multiples

slides.notes: 2 min. The 2025 deck's "Design choices" and "When designing with animation": define purpose, match task to interaction, choose transitions carefully, test with users.

slides.name: 74 · Move responsibly

params.text: A reader controls the clock: a slider, a play button, a reset.
Small multiples or the last frame, for print and for analysis.
Respect prefers-reduced-motion: jump to the end (WCAG 2.3.3).
Axes that never move, so only the data does.

76 · Four things to keep

params.text: Interaction answers the reader's question, not yours: start from a persona.
Show less and let them ask, but never hide the message in a tooltip.
One choice can light every view: input, parameter, predicate, response.
Motion is seen first; spend it on change, and keep identity with key=.
